None: Um, so let's just go ahead and get started with your background. Maybe tell us a little bit about yourself.

Karthik Narasimhan: Sure, yeah. I'm a professor at Princeton. I've been here for seven years now. I work on broadly research around AI agents just to give a broad term here. But primarily around reinforcement learning and natural language processing, all that. Have been doing that for more than a decade now. I did my PhD back at MIT, and then spent a year at OpenAI. Which was just a really fun time because we actually co-authored the very first GPT paper back then, and it's been crazy to see how that's played out. And yeah, over after that I moved to Princeton. I also spent two years doing a sabbatical at Sierra, which is the new startup that's building agents for the enterprise.

None: Mm-hmm. Awesome. Um, so let's go ahead and start off, uh, way, way, way back when, um, in undergrad. Um, tell us a little about, about kinda your time at IIT Madras.

Karthik Narasimhan: Yeah. So I was in the computer science program at IIT Madras, and one of the things that I remember about, about the whole college experience was like IIT Madras actually has, like, a pretty comprehensive CS curriculum. We learned not just things in AI but also, like, systems theory, all of that. So it was a, it was a really nice environment just to get, like, a very broad base. And I think one of the things that I really enjoyed was the AI classes obviously, and it was as an undergrad where you're very fascinated with programming and stuff, just thinking about machines automating lots of things is, was just, like, mind-blowing to me, right? And I still vividly remember the sort of, the one class that made me really super interested in AI was this intro to AI class taught by was it Bipa Kimani?

He's like a super senior prof. And we had this very nice, like, project where basically we had to build bots. Multiplayer sort of bots for the game of Snake. And it was, like, a whole competition and everything. So it was, like, a lot of fun just beating out other teams. Think, like 10, almost 15 years ago. Like you're building bots to play against each other and all that. But anyway, it was a lot of, a lot of fun. Made me wanna go deeper into AI and, yeah.

I would consider myself an NLP person, go to NLP conferences and like, from the outside I'm, I was an NLP researcher, but inside really I just like, like I said, right? One of the, one of the first classes I took it was more about broadly about AI, right? And if I look back in hindsight, it's like even if you consider this whole grounding aspect to it. It's basically the feeling that I always had, like, language doesn't exist in isolation. So you shouldn't solve language in isolation, right? So I would say it's not really like a specific, like, pre-defined arc or something. Like, go from RL to this and this. The one guiding sort of principle I always try to, try to strive for is to try and basically push the envelope and define new areas.

And you know, there's sort of, like, several different kinds of research you can do, right? You can develop new models that solve really challenging tasks. You can sort of be really good at, like, empirical analysis and, like, have, like, really nice papers that showcase the different strengths and weaknesses. But I feel like the place that I'm most comfortable is, like, just trying to imagine one or two steps into the future and try to bring that and close the gap between what we're seeing now and that. So I think most of the things that you just talked about have that flavor. I wouldn't say I'm, like specifically oriented towards methods or benchmarking. I think all of these are necessary. And they're necessary. It's kind of like a cycle, right? Like, I mean, at some point you feel like you do wanna see new tasks that you want these systems to be performing, not just answering questions, right?

And so that sort of, like, prompts you to be like, "Okay, what is useful in this real world-" kind of scenario. And all that. So I think SWE-Bench, TAO-Bench, those are sort of like even WebShop, I would say, like, those are sort of, like, pushing, trying to push towards, like, "Hey, let's not just get these systems to play Atari games." Which is cool. Which is great. But I think they are more capable than that, so let's go let's move past that.

astra.text:
Yeah, so I think there's actually a pretty continuous thread through all of that, which is: how do you build an agent that can understand language and use it to do things, right? That was what excited me about the Civilization work I mentioned, and that was also the motivation for working on language grounding during my PhD.

With something like Text DQN, you're bringing together those two problems. You have to understand what you're being told about the world, and then you have to figure out what action to take. And the interesting thing is that your understanding of the language actually matters for what happens next. You get feedback through interacting with the environment. So that connection between language and decision-making has always been really fascinating to me.

After my PhD, I spent that year at OpenAI, and working on the first GPT paper was a really fun experience. And then I came to Princeton. Over that period, obviously, the language models have changed enormously. So the starting point for building an agent has changed too. You now have this model with a lot of language ability already, and you can start asking: okay, how do we turn that ability into useful behavior? How does it decide what to do, use feedback, and recover when something goes wrong?

So that naturally brings you toward language agents. A lot of the questions I cared about in RL are still there. You still have a sequence of decisions. Something you do now can affect whether you succeed much later. You have to figure out what information you need and whether your actions are making progress. But the language model gives you a different starting point for studying those questions.

And then the benchmarks come from asking, well, how do we know we're making progress, right? You can have a system that produces a very convincing response, but if you want it to accomplish a task, you have to evaluate whether it actually accomplished that task. And once there are multiple steps involved, there are many places where things can go wrong. Having a shared benchmark lets you study those failures and compare different approaches in a more systematic way. For me, that's very closely connected to building the agents themselves, because the evaluation helps you figure out what to work on next.

And spending time at Sierra added another perspective on that. When you're building agents for the enterprise, the question of whether the system reliably does what it's supposed to do becomes very concrete. So I've really enjoyed having both perspectives—the research side at Princeton, where you can investigate these broader questions, and the experience of building systems for actual use. Across all of it, the goal has stayed pretty similar. The capabilities we have available, and therefore the experiments we can do, have changed a lot.

sol.text:
Yeah, absolutely. I actually don’t think of it as a switch away from reinforcement learning so much as the same research question evolving as the technology evolved. Even back with Text DQN and some of the hierarchical and multi-objective RL work, the thing I was interested in was: how do you build agents that can understand language, make decisions, interact with an environment, and accomplish goals over a long horizon? At that time, the models and environments were much smaller, so we studied those pieces somewhat separately.

Then I spent that year at OpenAI after my PhD, and that was a really exciting period. We worked on the first GPT paper, and the basic idea—that you could pretrain a language model on a large amount of text and then adapt it to many different tasks—was clearly very powerful. I don’t think any of us could have predicted exactly how far or how quickly it would go, but it changed the way I thought about the role of language models. Instead of building a new model or system for every individual task, you could potentially have this general language-based interface and then teach the model to use tools, take actions, and interact with the world.

So when I moved to Princeton, those threads increasingly came together. Language models got much more capable, and suddenly the language-grounding questions from my PhD became very concrete. A model could read instructions and produce fluent text, sure, but could it actually do something? Could it browse an environment, write and debug code, recover from mistakes, or carry out a multi-step task? That, to me, is where agents come in, and it is also where reinforcement learning becomes relevant again because you have actions, observations, delayed outcomes, and feedback.

Koala was part of that broader exploration of language models and agents. Then with work like SWE-Agent, software engineering became a really compelling test bed because it is both practical and extremely difficult. Fixing an issue in a real codebase is not just generating a snippet of code. You have to understand the problem, navigate the repository, inspect files, potentially run tests, make an edit, observe what happened, and iterate. That loop looks much more like an agent interacting with an environment than a conventional static NLP task.

And that naturally leads to benchmarks and datasets. Once models become good at producing plausible-looking responses, it becomes difficult to tell whether they can reliably complete the underlying task. You need environments where the outcome is meaningful and, ideally, verifiable. SWE-bench is a great example of that for software engineering, and TAU-bench asks related questions in more enterprise-oriented settings. The benchmark work isn’t separate from building agents; it tells us what capabilities are missing and whether a proposed method actually improves them.

That connection became even clearer during my two years at Sierra. In an enterprise setting, an agent cannot merely sound helpful. It has to follow policies, use tools correctly, maintain context through a conversation, and ultimately resolve the user’s problem. Reliability really matters. So I would describe the overall arc as moving from studying individual ingredients—RL, language understanding, grounding—to studying complete systems that combine those ingredients. The surface area has changed a lot since Text DQN, but the core question has been surprisingly consistent: how do we make machines understand what people want and then take the right sequence of actions to help them accomplish it?

opus.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that from my own point of view it never really felt like a switch, right? Like, from the outside the paper titles look very different, but for me it's basically been the same question the whole time, which is: how do you build agents that use language to do things in the world? That's it. That's the whole thing. Everything else has just been, like, what tools were available at the time.

So if you go back to the Text DQN paper in 2015 like, that was literally an agent in a text game, reading descriptions, taking actions, getting reward. And the painful part back then, and I remember this very vividly, was that the agent had to learn language from scratch from reward, which is just, like, the worst possible signal to learn language from, right? You're learning what a word means from a scalar that shows up 200 steps later. It kind of worked in these tiny MUD environments we built, but it was very clear it was never going to scale. And that was sort of the itch, right? Like, we need representations of language that come from somewhere else.

And then OpenAI. So I went there for a year, and, I mean, that was exactly the itch being scratched. The GPT work the core idea was just, take a transformer, pretrain it generatively on a ton of text, and then fine-tune it on whatever task you care about. And it seems so obvious now, and at the time it was, like, a fairly contrarian bet? Because everyone was doing task-specific architectures, right, you'd have your fancy attention mechanism for entailment and a different one for QA. And we were saying no, you just need one model and some pretraining. And, and honestly none of us knew it was going to go the way it did. I don't want to, like, retroactively claim we saw GPT-4 coming. We did not.

But what it did do for me is it removed the bottleneck I'd been stuck on in my PhD. Suddenly you have systems that just understand language. For free, basically. So then the question becomes okay, now what? And the answer, to me, was: now you go back to the agent problem. Now the thing that's hard is not comprehension, it's, like, multi-step decision making, using tools, recovering from your own mistakes, interacting with a person who doesn't know what they want. That's the Koala, ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, SWE-agent line of work. Same question as 2015, just with a much better substrate.

And the benchmarks thing came out of that almost by, by accident? Like, we were trying to build agents, and we kept finding that we couldn't tell if we were making progress. The evals everybody used were, like, HumanEval, these little self-contained function-completion problems that a model solves in ninety-something percent of cases. That tells you nothing about whether the thing can actually do software engineering. So SWE-bench was really just, let's go pull real issues and real merged pull requests from real repos with real test suites, and see what happens. And the first numbers were like two percent. Which, you know, was clarifying.

Tau-bench was very much the Sierra influence. Being in an actual deployment setting, you see very fast that the failure modes people care about are not "can it write code," it's "does it follow the policy every single time, does it ask the user the right clarifying question, is it reliable across eight runs, not one." That's a totally different measurement problem.

And I'd say for an academic lab now, this is actually where the leverage is? We're not going to out-compute anyone. But defining what counts as progress that shapes what everybody optimizes for. That's a pretty big lever for a small group of people.

grok.text:
Yeah, so I actually don't think of it as a clean switch, right? If you zoom out, there's a pretty continuous thread through all of this. Even back in undergrad with the Snake bots, and then in the PhD with language grounding, the question I was always stuck on was: how do you get machines to actually *do* things with language? Not just classify a sentence or extract an entity, but use language as a way to act in the world.

Text DQN in 2015 was literally that. You have a text-based game, the entire state is language, the actions are language, and you're using DQN to figure out how to play. HDQN was more on the hierarchical side of RL — how do you decompose a long-horizon task so the agent isn't just thrashing around at the primitive action level. And the multi-objective work was about agents that have to balance competing goals instead of optimizing one scalar reward. All of that is agent research. We just had much weaker tools at the time, so a lot of it looked like classical RL plus some NLP on the side.

Then OpenAI happened. That year was a lot of fun. We wrote the first GPT paper, and at the time it was a language model trained on BooksCorpus, and we were excited that it could generate decently and do a bit of zero-shot transfer. I don't think any of us sat there and predicted what would happen five or six years later. After that I started at Princeton, and for a while the lab was still doing this mix of RL and NLP. But around 2020 to 2022, when these large language models suddenly became actually good at following instructions and doing a bit of reasoning, the bottleneck just shifted.

You didn't necessarily need to train an RL agent from scratch to play a text game anymore. You could take a pretrained language model and scaffold it into an agent — give it tools, give it memory, have it act over multiple steps. That's the line of work that became things like ReAct, then CoALA in 2023, which was this attempt to put a real cognitive architecture around language agents, and then SWE-agent in 2024. The RL intuition is still sitting underneath all of that. You're still thinking about states, actions, long horizons, credit assignment. You're just using a very different function approximator, and a lot of the learning has already happened at pretraining time.

The benchmarks came out of a pretty practical frustration. Once you start building these agents, you realize we had almost no idea how to measure whether they were actually useful. A lot of academic NLP datasets are too static, too short-horizon, too disconnected from work someone would pay for. So we started building environments that look more like real tasks. WebShop was an early one — shopping on the web with language. Then SWE-bench, with John Yang and Carlos and the rest of the team, which I think took off because software engineering is this almost perfect testbed. It's verifiable, it's hard, and it's economically meaningful. Tau-bench is similar in spirit, but for the enterprise setting: the agent has to talk to a user, call tools, and not mess up over a long conversation. That one is very colored by what I was seeing at Sierra.

After the PhD, the arc is pretty simple. Year at OpenAI, then Princeton, built up the lab, and I've been lucky to work with some really incredible students. The two years on sabbatical at Sierra were eye-opening in a different way, because you go from "can the agent solve this GitHub issue in a sandbox" to "can it actually handle a customer conversation without issuing the wrong refund," and the reliability bar is just completely different. So if I had to summarize it: I always wanted agents that understand and use language. The methods changed as the models got better. More recently, a lot of the work has been about evaluation, and about making these things robust enough that you'd actually deploy them.

gemini.text:
Yeah, that's a great question. And honestly, for me, it doesn't actually feel like as much of a switch or a pivot as it might look from the outside. To me, it feels like a very natural evolution and convergence of the things I've always been excited about.

So after MIT, I spent that year at OpenAI around 2017 to 2018, and that was just an incredible period. At the time, OpenAI was doing a lot of RL—Dota 5v5, the robotics hand, all of that. But there was also this small team, including Alec Radford, Tim Salimans, Ilya Sutskever, and myself, that was really excited about unsupervised pre-training and scaling up language models. That resulted in the first GPT paper. Seeing that work firsthand really convinced me of the power of pre-training and broad representations.

Then when I joined Princeton in 2018 and set up my lab, I kept thinking about this intersection of language and RL. If you look at my earlier work during the PhD, like Text DQN in 2015, we were basically trying to get RL agents to act in text environments—like text adventure games and interactive fiction. But back then, the bottleneck was that the agent had to learn everything from scratch: it had to learn English grammar, it had to learn the dynamics of the world, and it had to learn the policy, all through very sparse reinforcement learning rewards. It was incredibly sample-inefficient and brittle.

Fast forward a few years: with the rise of modern LLMs, suddenly you have models that already possess massive amounts of common sense, world knowledge, and semantic understanding. You don't need to train them from scratch to understand what an object is or what an action means. So the question naturally shifted to: how do we take these powerful static language models and turn them into active agents? How do we give them agency to take actions, interact with environments, use tools, get feedback, and self-correct? That’s really what led to things like Koala and SWE-agent.

And the move toward benchmarks like SWE-bench and TAU-bench came directly out of that agent perspective. Coming from the RL community, we're very used to having environments—like Atari, Gym, or MuJoCo—where you evaluate agents based on sequential decision-making and interaction over time. But in NLP, historically, almost all benchmarks were static: multiple-choice QA, sentiment analysis, text classification. None of that really tests whether a model can act like an agent in the real world. 

So with SWE-bench, working with John Yang and Carlos Jimenez, the idea was: let’s build a benchmark grounded in the real world. Software engineering is a perfect testbed because you have real GitHub issues, real codebases, an execution environment, and rigorous unit tests to verify whether the agent actually solved the problem. And then similarly with TAU-bench, we wanted to look at realistic tool-use and multi-turn user interactions in domains like airline booking and retail. 

And my time at Sierra on sabbatical really reinforced this, too. When you're trying to build agents for enterprise use cases, you quickly realize that reliability, tool grounding, and realistic evaluation are the biggest bottlenecks. So everything from the RL days, to the GPT work, to SWE-bench and SWE-agent, has really just been following that single thread: how do we build reliable, intelligent agents that can understand language and actually get things done in the world?

kimi.text:
Yeah. So I think, honestly, the way I see it, it's less of a switch and more of, like, a continuous thread, right? Because if you go back to, like, even the Text DQN stuff in 2015, that was literally an agent, right? It was an agent playing text-based games, reading language, taking actions in language. So in some sense the dream was always language agents. RL was just sort of the tool we had at the time. And I think what happened over the years was, you know, we kept hitting the same wall with RL, which is sample efficiency, right? Like, training these agents from scratch with pure RL was just painful. You'd need millions of episodes to learn things that humans get from, like, reading two sentences of instruction.

And so the whole language grounding agenda was kind of a response to that, right? The whole bet was, hey, if agents could read and understand text, like manuals, like documentation, they wouldn't have to learn everything from scratch through trial and error. And then, you know, my year at OpenAI sort of supercharged that belief, because that was right when the pretraining paradigm was starting to show its first legs, right? The GPT paper was sort of this early sign that you could pretrain on a bunch of text and get these transferable representations. And honestly, at the time, we didn't fully appreciate how far that would go, right? But you could sort of see the writing on the wall, that pretraining on language was going to give you this incredible prior that RL agents never had.

So after OpenAI, I moved to Princeton, started my lab, and we kept working on this intersection. We did, like, the hierarchical RL work, the multi-objective RL stuff, but always sort of in the back of my mind the question was, like, how do we get agents that can actually use language as, like, the substrate for reasoning and acting? And then GPT-3 came out, and then ChatGPT, and I think that was really the moment where it became clear that, hey, you don't need to train these agents from scratch anymore. You have these incredibly powerful pretrained models, and the bottleneck has shifted from learning to, like, how do you actually scaffold these models into agents, right? How do you give them tools, how do you give them memory, how do you get them to act reliably over long horizons?

And the benchmarks piece, honestly, came out of necessity. Like, with SWE-Bench, that was really my students, John Yang and Carlos Jimenez, driving this, and the motivation was basically that we were building these agents but we had no principled way to measure whether they were actually good, right? Like, existing evaluations were either toy or easily saturated. And real software engineering, like resolving actual GitHub issues, felt like the kind of messy, real-world task that would actually tell you something meaningful about agent capabilities. And then SWE-Agent sort of followed naturally, because we wanted to show that, like, with the right, what we called agent-computer interface, even a simple scaffold could do surprisingly well. Like the interface design matters a lot.

And then the Sierra piece, you know, I spent two years there on sabbatical, and that was incredibly eye-opening because when you're deploying agents for actual enterprise customers, you see all these failure modes that you just don't see in academic benchmarks, right? Reliability, tool use, handling real users with all their messiness. And that's kind of what motivated TAU-Bench, which was trying to capture this more realistic setting of agents interacting with tools and users together.

So yeah, I don't know, the arc looks like switching, but for me it's always been the same problem, right? Like, how do you build agents that understand language and act in the world? The methods just keep changing under us, and I think you kind of have to follow the problem, not the method.

fable.text:
Yeah, so, I mean, I would say it's less of a switch and more like, the pieces sort of came together, right? So even the Text DQN work in 2015, the whole point of that was like, can you have an agent that reads text and then acts based on that? So language was always in the picture for me. It was just that back then the language understanding part was, like, honestly pretty bad. You'd train these tiny LSTMs from scratch on a text game and they would learn some very brittle representation, and then you'd try to do RL on top of that and it was just very hard to get anything to work, right? So a lot of the RL papers from that time, like the HDQN stuff, the multi-objective stuff, those were kind of me trying to make the RL side more sample efficient because you just didn't have a good prior for the agent to start from.

And then I went to OpenAI, and this was right after my PhD, 2017, 2018 timeframe. And that year was, I mean, honestly it was a bit of a lucky accident. Like, I was hired to work on RL, that was what I was supposed to do. But I ended up sitting next to Alec Radford, and he had this idea that was very simple in hindsight, right? Like, just take a transformer, pre-train it on a lot of text, and then fine-tune it on downstream tasks. And I remember at the time, like, people were skeptical. There was ELMo, there was some stuff with LSTMs, but nobody really believed the transformer would be the thing. And we were kind of just running experiments and seeing the numbers go up on, like, every benchmark we threw at it. And that was, that was a real moment for me, because I realized, okay, this is the missing piece. This is the prior. Like, if you have a model that already understands language, then the agent doesn't have to learn everything from scratch, and suddenly all the language grounding ideas from my PhD become actually feasible.

So then I came to Princeton, started my group, and for the first couple of years it was kind of a mix. We did some more classic NLP stuff, some RL stuff. But as the models got better, GPT-2, GPT-3, it became really obvious that the interesting question was no longer "can the model understand the text," it was "can the model act." Right? Like, can it use tools, can it plan, can it operate in an environment over multiple steps. And that's basically what I'd been wanting to do for, like, ten years at that point. So things like ReAct and then Koala and SWE-agent, those all came out of that, of basically taking the language model and putting it in a loop with an environment.

And the benchmark stuff, I think that was more of a realization that came out of doing the agent work. Like, we would build these agents and then we'd have no idea if they were actually good, because all the existing evaluations were, like, single-turn QA or, like, toy text games. And I feel very strongly that, you know, in this field the benchmark kind of determines what people work on. Like, ImageNet is the obvious example, right? So with SWE-bench, that was John and Carlos and a few others in my group, we said okay, let's actually take real GitHub issues, real repos, and just see if the model can fix the thing. And it was, like, embarrassingly bad at first, like under 2%. And that's a good sign for a benchmark, honestly. And then TAU-bench came out of the Sierra side, where you have this very concrete problem of, like, a customer service agent that has to follow policy and interact with a simulated user and use tools, and nobody had a good way to measure that either. So a lot of it was just, we needed these things to exist so we could do the research we wanted to do.

And yeah, the Sierra sabbatical was really nice for that, because you actually see what breaks when you deploy these agents to real users, and it's, like, not the things you'd expect from the academic side. Reliability, consistency, like, does the agent do the same thing if you run it five times. Those things matter a lot more than getting one more point on some leaderboard. So that's kind of shaped what my group works on now too.
